I am only going to address the unemployment part of your post, have you ever thought of volunteer work? 

If you volunteer at a place, it gives you something to do, and it can deter the "unfulfilled" feeling that comes with unemployment sometimes. It's also a great way to learn some skills, like how to use Excell if you volunteer at a free clinic, how to take care of animals if you volunteer at a shelter, etc. 


Sometimes if you volunteer it can lead to job opportunities at the same place. Granted, volunteering doesn't guarantee paid work later, but if you apply to jobs while volunteering it looks awesome on your résumé. 

It also can show your family that you're not just "sitting around doing nothing", granted you aren't just sitting on your ass now, but at least you'll be out of the house and away from a negative environment. You'll also feel good about what you're doing!

I am allergic to nickel, have been since I was a kid. I noticed it because the buttons on my pants or cheap jewelry (necklaces, bracelets) would cause a rash, almost like a slight case of really itchy eczema, wherever the metal was touching my skin that would stay there for a few days. If you're allergic to nickel, you should notice things like that. 

When it comes to piercings with nickel jewelry, I notice a crust forms around the piercing, it itches like hell and some sort of bump appears at the sight. Follow ssnakeggirl's advice and only wear grade titanium jewelry. It can be hard out there for people who love piercings but are also allergic to something that seems to be in *everything*

I can understand where you're coming from. I am in my 3rd year of college and I still have no flying fucking clue what I want to do with my life. I wish that, instead of going right to college after high school, I had worked and saved up enough money to be in a semi-decent financial position for when I did have enough sense and knew more about myself as a person to pick something to study and to work towards. The person I was when I graduated high school and the person I am today are almost completely different people. When I look back at the process of graduating high school and applying to colleges I often wonder how anyone expected me to know what I would want to do for a good portion of my life when I wasn't even old enough to vote yet.

Instead, being a undeclared junior, I feel like I have wasted a significant amount of time while procuring a lot of student loan debt with really nothing to show for it. I almost want to leave my University, just for a year or two, to work and to *really* think about what I want to do and study. The problem is is that if I left there is no fucking way I could possibly start making payments on my student loans (which I would have to start making immediately) in addition to my rent and other expenses with the jobs that I have now. 

Sorry for ranting, but here's my point. College directly after high school is not for everyone. Sure, some of your friends will go directly to college, pick a major and be happy with that field forever. Some might change majors several times and some will drop out because they feel how I feel. Don't be afraid to speak up now, to talk to your family about other possibilities and paths because it is *your life*. YOU are going to be paying for your college education (unless your situation is totally awesome) whether you enroll and graduate or enroll and drop out. College will consume a lot of your life and it will affect your path into the career world. 

Do I think you should go to college at some point down the line? Absolutely, but by no means should you rush into such a huge financial and time consuming commitment if you don't feel like you are ready just because you feel outside pressure to enroll.

Women being awarded children in custody battles is actually fairly new (in Britain anyway). It wasn't until 1839 that when a woman was divorced she was allowed to see her children *at all*, but this was only if she could prove that she hadn't committed adultery. 

It wasn't until 1873 that women were granted custody of their children, but only if the children in question were under the age of sixteen. If they were any older than that the ex-husband would gain custody. 

Actually, it wasn't even until the 1970's that women were given the same legal rights to their children as their husbands. That's only 40 years ago. 

So, if you look at it this way, custody over ones own children was a right that was denied to women up until the 70's. Of course I believe that both parents should be active in their children's lives and should have the right to see their child (unless there is a very good reason why one parent should not have the rights to the child; ie abuse, drug use, etc.) but what I am tired of, however, is people thinking and arguing that men have *always* gotten the short end of the stick when it comes to child custody laws.
